title: Playing with Vic Pellegrini and his father at an Elysian Fields dance hall
summary: Hirsch worked as a teen with Vic Pellegrini and his father at a dance hall, and recalls Vic's later life.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Did he play trumpet, Vic, the young one?
No, the young Vic Pellegrini was a piano player. Okay. He goes by the name now of Victor Pell. Victor Pell. He was, in later years he became Blossom Seely's accompanist. Ah, okay.

Yeah, I know that. Later years she became a partner. And he was down here, I worked with them, we used to play in a dance hall down on Elysium Fields. You have to go out on the gallery and play a warm up tune to get the customers to come in. And I don't remember who the hell was playing the piano but I know Vic was playing piano. I don't think we had a bass fiddle. We had a trombone and his father played the carnet. I don't remember who played trombone but these were all adults. And Vic and I, we were still in Warren Easton High School. We were still in high school and this was before 1926 when I graduated from Warren Easton. And I played with them for quite a few years. And then Vic went away and he went to New York. He went on the stage. He was down here, oh maybe ten years or so ago. And oddly enough, I was talking to him about when we were up in, he was in the food process, the food business. He was, we were up in, out of Baltimore, eastern Maryland. And when we were up there for a wedding, his friend of mine, we went to a restaurant, I wanted to eat clams, and we went to a restaurant that was like on a bay up there. And it was an old restaurant from the Civil War, from the Revolutionary War and all of that stuff. And we had lunch in there. And oddly enough, I told Vic that when he came down here on a visit and he called me, and I took him all around. Then later, he was, had charge of a big, well you could call them condominiums now, in Washington, D.C. or somewhere maybe in Virginia. That he was in charge of all of this and he had to build kitchens and this and that and the next thing. And it was a big deal. So I took him to the Rivergate and I showed him the kitchens down there and I showed him the kitchens of the Roosevelt Hotel when they were just adding on to the Imperial Ballroom. And we got, we had him out here a couple of times for dinner and renewed our acquaintanceship. And I told him about eastern Maryland, up in Maryland. He said, you know, it's a funny thing, I used to own that place. I sold it. There was some guy that was the, one of the benefits or the donors of the benefactors, and donors of the American Revolution. His name was Morris. The guy, his name was Morris. He was one of the benefactors of the American Revolution. He raised the money. He used to own that place. And I haven't, I haven't heard from Dick in quite a while. But I don't think he's on stage anymore because I mean, I don't think Barterfield's on stage anymore.
